newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Sept 30.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Sept 30.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- EXCHANGE POSTPONES ORDER-DRIVEN SYSTEM

The Stock Exchange's plan to move to order driven share trading, being introduced despite initial opposition from most large market-making firms, is being put back six months, to the final quarter of 1997. The proposal to be published this week follows two consultation processes conducted among market users this year. The delay is being partly blamed on the Treasury
which has yet to clarify some rules.
-- BA ON COURSE FOR 1 BILLION STG A YEAR PROFITS

City forecasts that British Airways will be making around 1.0 billion stg profit a year by the end of the decade have been endorsed by BA's manager of financial strategy and investor relations. Talking at a presentation to staff justifying the need for another 1.0 billion stg of cost cuts he said that analysts' forecasts of an annual increases in profits of around 12 percent are not unreasonable.
-- RETAILING LEADS THE WAY WITH NEW JOBS

The latest survey by the Manpower employment recruitment group shows that job prospects are continuing to improve and that the retailing industry is leading the way. The survey shows that 64 percent of retailers expect to hire more staff over the coming three months. Over a quarter of all employers surveyed said they expect to take on more staff before the end of the year, with 10 percent predicting cutbacks.
THE TIMES
-- WATCHDOG WOULD WELCOME SCOTTISH SALE BY BRITISH GAS

The prospect of British Gas selling its gas supply business in Scotland and the north of England to Scottish Hydro- Electric was welcomed yesterday by the Gas Consumers Council. The Gas Consumers Council said the sale would be a win-win deal for consumers and the two companies.
-- CLARKE'S GOLD SCHEME WINS IMF SUPPORT

A plan first proposed by Kenneth Clarke, the Chancellor has been given the go-ahead by the International Monetary Fund's ruling Interim Committee. The debt plan first proposed at the Commonwealth finance ministers' meeting in Malta two years ago, will eventually provide about $6 billion worth of help to 20 developing countries which have started economic reform programmes but still have very large debts to official creditors like the IMF and World Bank.
-- UNIONS HAVE SENT 100 MLN STG LABOUR'S WAY SINCE 1979

A study by the Times out today shows that trade unions have spent over 100 million stg at 1995 prices in funding the Labour Party since 1979. The trade unions' share of Labour's income is likely to be close to 40 percent in 1997 which is around half of its level when Labour was last in power. The trade unions support amounts to only around one percent of Labour's total spending.
THE GUARDIAN
-- BR TRUST CARPETS TREASURY CHIEF

Senior Treasury officer Chris Daykin has been carpeted for revealing in advance the potential surpluses of British Rail's 13 billion pension scheme to bidders for key parts of the rail network. Daykin, the government actuary, has agreed to meet the BR fund trustees to explain why he failed to alert them to what he was doing.
-- STATE REBUFF FOR SELF-HELP SCHEME

The Department of Social Security is blocking plans to give the unemployed a route back to work through barter schemes. A study published at the weekend shows that the DSS has threatened to suspend payments to unemployed people who take part in Lets, local exchange trading systems. According to the study by the New Economics Foundation the Lets scheme offered a route back to work and has been successful in housing estate areas in Manchester, Glasgow, Cardiff, Wrexham and Hull.
-- IMF AIMS AT CAPITAL MARKETS
Reform of the International
Monetary Fund was closer
yesterday as plans were announced that would give the agency

more money and power. A UK initiative that would give the IMF authority to encourage the liberalisation and stability of capital markets, won the support of financial lenders. Leading industrial countries believe that there is a need to balance new freedoms in the world financial markets with tougher bank supervision and financial regulation.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- US FEARS SINGLE CURRENCY WILL SLOW EUROPEAN GROWTH

At the G7 meeting in Washington this weekend the US focused on the implications of the single European currency for the world economy, expressing the belief that lower interest rates in Europe will avert the danger that tighter budgets will slow growth. The meeting also produced a consensus that the world economy is in a satisfactory state and that most regions have non-inflationary growth.
-- BASS JOINS THE RUSH TO THE THEMED BAR

Bass has joined Britain's other large leisure companies, Whitbread and Rank, in the rush to buy up the themed bar and restaurant sector. It has been revealed that Bass were unsuccessful in a bid to buy the Pitcher & Piano chain of bars earlier this year. Marston, Thompson & Evershed secured the seven outlets in June. Bass are committed to the rapid expansion of its fast growing All Bar One bars which are bright and modern and aimed at young, trendy drinkers and also have a high level of food sales.
-- YOUNG WAS ACTING ALONE, SFO BELIEVES

The Serious Fraud Office who are working on the Morgan Grenfell unit trust scandal believe that Peter Young was acting alone, dismissing speculation that he was part of a criminal conspiracy. The SFO is now working to establish whether Young has committed any criminal offence.
